quality_rationale: The proposal earns credit for an original, actionable topic, a detailed multimodal collection plan, and sensible reproducibility and privacy practices. However, its central wear measure lacks independent physical ground truth and is partly defined by endogenous replacement behavior. It then uses this circular proxy in under-specified observational models, overstates effective sample size, overlooks key clustering, and converts associations into causal policy simulations. Arbitrary thresholds and an unvalidated composite index further weaken inference. These are foundational problems despite the polished structure and practical detail, supporting an anchor near 30.
planted_strengths: The proposal identifies a genuinely novel and practically relevant sports-analytics question: continuous measurement of shuttle wear through impact acoustics rather than treating equipment condition as constant.
It specifies a useful multimodal data-collection system with synchronized audio, video, score, shuttle identity, and racket-motion data, along with concrete coding and data-quality procedures.

It includes worthwhile reproducibility and privacy provisions, including preregistration, blinded video coding, release of analysis scripts and derived features, and withholding identifiable raw video.
planted_weaknesses: The Shuttle Age Acoustic Score is trained to predict normalized position within a use cycle, but cycle length is determined by endogenous player and umpire replacement decisions. The score can therefore learn shot selection, game context, or replacement behavior rather than physical wear; post-match photographs do not provide an independent physical validation.

The proposal repeatedly gives causal interpretations to observational associations. Shuttle age, score progression, player fatigue, tactics, replacement requests, and point outcomes all evolve together, and the proposed covariates and within-match comparisons do not identify the causal effect of wear. The policy simulator compounds this problem by treating fitted associations as intervention effects.

The power calculation and outcome models substantially understate dependence. Thousands of strokes are treated as an enormous effective sample even though impacts are nested within rallies, shuttle cycles, games, matches, and a small set of 24 players. Assigning the same rally result to every stroke and accounting only for match random effects creates pseudo-replication.

Several choices are arbitrary or weakly justified, including the 18-impact change point, SAAS threshold of 0.65, five-impact AEI windows, 10% meaningful-loss rule, and policy utility weight. The multiplicative Attacking Efficiency Index has no validation and mixes tactical choice, speed, and outcome.

Measurement validity is insufficiently addressed: acoustic features are strongly affected by racket, contact quality, shot type, microphone selection, and hall conditions, while swing speed is estimated from uncalibrated sensors on players' own rackets. Mean imputation of missing exit speeds can further bias the flight analysis.
topic: Using racket–shuttle impact acoustics to estimate feather-shuttle deterioration and model its effects on badminton tactics, outcomes, and replacement policy.
title: Listening for Feather Fatigue: Acoustic Detection of Shuttle Wear and Its Tactical Effects in Competitive Badminton

# Listening for Feather Fatigue: Acoustic Detection of Shuttle Wear and Its Tactical Effects in Competitive Badminton

## Abstract

Feather shuttles deteriorate during play, but their condition is normally judged through player inspection, flight feel, and negotiation with the umpire. This proposal investigates whether the sound of racket–shuttle contact can provide an objective measure of shuttle wear and whether accumulating wear changes tactics or point outcomes. The study will create a purpose-organized badminton competition, the Northbridge Indoor Series, involving 24 advanced club players and 72 singles matches. Four directional microphones, two high-speed cameras, and racket-mounted motion sensors will record approximately 24,000 strokes.

An acoustic model called the Shuttle Age Acoustic Score (SAAS) will be trained to predict how far a shuttle has progressed through its use cycle. Spectral brightness, attack duration, high-frequency roll-off, harmonic concentration, and impact loudness will be extracted from each contact. The proposal hypothesizes that higher SAAS values will be associated with reduced shuttle exit speed, greater use of clears and drops relative to smashes, and an advantage for the player who first requests a replacement. Multilevel models will relate acoustic age to stroke choice and point success. The resulting estimates will also be used in a simulator comparing replacement policies based on fixed numbers of impacts, acoustic thresholds, or existing player-led decisions.

The project addresses an overlooked equipment variable and offers a method that could operate without interrupting play. It will produce a synchronized stroke-level dataset, an open feature-extraction pipeline, and recommendations for tournament organizers. The central premise is that the natural progression of a shuttle from new to worn functions as a repeated within-match exposure, allowing the sporting effects of wear to be estimated more precisely than through occasional laboratory flight tests.

## 1. Background and rationale

Badminton analytics usually emphasizes player movement, shot placement, rally length, and match score. The shuttle is commonly treated as a stable object until it is replaced. In practice, feather tips bend, separate, or break after repeated impacts. Players often inspect a shuttle between rallies and may ask the umpire to change it. A request can be accepted, refused, or disputed by the opponent. These decisions matter because a worn shuttle may travel differently, yet there is no continuous, neutral record of its condition.

This gap has two consequences. First, tactical analyses may attribute a change in shot selection to fatigue or score pressure when part of the change comes from equipment. Second, replacement rules are based on visible damage and player judgment rather than a consistent performance threshold. A system capable of listening to impacts could potentially indicate when a shuttle has crossed such a threshold.

Impact acoustics are a promising source because every legal stroke generates a short, information-rich signal. A fresh shuttle has a compact skirt and relatively consistent feather alignment. Repeated deformation should alter how the cork and skirt vibrate after contact. In principle, these changes may affect the attack and decay of the recorded sound. Acoustic monitoring would also be cheaper than installing a complete ball-tracking system in every venue.

The proposal concentrates on match play rather than laboratory aerodynamics. This is important because shuttle deterioration is produced by the same mixture of smashes, slices, net shots, and accidental frame contacts that defines competition. Laboratory launchers can deliver repeatable impacts but do not reproduce tactical variation. The study therefore treats each shuttle-use cycle—from introduction to replacement or the end of a game—as a miniature longitudinal experiment.

Coaches commonly claim that worn shuttles reward defensive players because they lose speed. An alternative possibility is that deformation makes flight less predictable and therefore benefits aggressive players. A third possibility is that the shuttle has little direct effect, but the act of requesting a replacement creates a pause that disrupts momentum. The proposed combination of audio, video, score state, and replacement records is intended to separate these explanations.

## 2. Research questions and hypotheses

The primary research question is:

> Can contact sound be used to measure feather-shuttle wear during live badminton, and does acoustically measured wear alter tactics and competitive outcomes?

Five hypotheses will be tested:

1. **H1: Acoustic aging.** SAAS will rise as the number of impacts on a shuttle increases, with the clearest separation after approximately 18 impacts.
2. **H2: Flight loss.** A one-standard-deviation increase in SAAS will predict lower shuttle exit speed after adjustment for racket swing speed and coded stroke type.
3. **H3: Tactical drift.** Players will use fewer full smashes and more clears, drops, and half-smashes as SAAS increases.
4. **H4: Request advantage.** The player who first requests a shuttle change will win a greater proportion of the next three points than the opponent, particularly when SAAS is high.
5. **H5: Replacement efficiency.** An automatic replacement rule triggered by SAAS will reduce tactically meaningful shuttle deterioration while using fewer shuttles than a fixed-impact rule.

The threshold of 18 impacts is based on informal preliminary recordings in which differences between early and late contacts became audible around that point. Impacts include serves and returns but exclude contacts during warm-up or when the shuttle is hit back to the server after a rally.

## 3. Study design

### 3.1 Competition and participants

The Northbridge Indoor Series will be a six-week purpose-organized singles competition at Veyra Sports Hall. Twenty-four advanced club players aged 18 to 35 will be recruited through regional clubs. Twelve places will be reserved for women and twelve for men. Participants must have played organized badminton for at least three years and must train at least twice per week.

Players will be divided into four pools of six based on self-reported competitive level. Each player will complete five pool matches and one classification match, producing 72 matches. Matches will use a best-of-three-games format to 21 points. The study is focused on within-player and within-shuttle changes, so differences between the men’s and women’s pools will not be a primary outcome.

All matches will use the same batch of the invented Aerius F12 tournament-grade feather shuttle. Players may use their normal rackets and strings so that strokes remain natural. Racket model, string material, reported tension, handedness, and grip size will be recorded before the first match. Tension will not be remeasured during the series unless a player reports restringing.

Two trained umpires will alternate matches. Existing replacement practice will be retained: a player may inspect the shuttle and request a change, the opponent may respond, and the umpire makes the final decision. No acoustic information will be shown to participants or umpires during play.

### 3.2 Shuttle tracking

Each shuttle will receive a small ink code on the inner cork before use. A court assistant will scan the code when the shuttle enters or leaves play. This will establish a use cycle and prevent a rejected shuttle from being accidentally counted as a new one. Replaced shuttles will be placed in numbered envelopes and photographed after the match from four angles.

The assistant will record one of four exit reasons: accepted player request, umpire-initiated replacement, visible catastrophic failure, or game completion. For accepted requests, the requesting player and whether the opponent initially agreed will be noted. Rejected requests will also be timestamped.

Photographs will be assigned a simple damage category—none, bent feather, separated feathers, or broken feather—by one project researcher. These categories will be used descriptively because acoustic condition, rather than visible damage, is the intended primary measure.

### 3.3 Sensor arrangement

Four directional microphones will be mounted at the corners of the court, 1.8 metres above the floor and outside the playing area. Audio will be recorded at 96 kHz. A synchronization pulse will be played before every game. Two cameras operating at 240 frames per second will capture lateral and rear views. An inertial sensor weighing less than six grams will be attached to each racket butt to estimate swing speed.

The custom CourtPulse logger will combine audio, video, score, and sensor timestamps. Automatic impact detection will identify sharp acoustic events occurring near a peak in racket acceleration. A research assistant will inspect uncertain events and remove shoe squeaks, claps, collisions with the floor, and simultaneous sounds from adjacent courts. Only one study court will operate at a time, although normal activity may continue on courts behind a divider.

Shuttle exit speed will be estimated from its displacement over the first eight camera frames after contact. Landing zone, contact location, and stroke type will be coded from video. Stroke types will be serve, clear, drop, drive, net shot, lift, full smash, half-smash, block, and unclassified. Twenty percent of matches will be coded by a second analyst, with agreement reported for stroke type and landing zone.

## 4. Constructing the Shuttle Age Acoustic Score

A 120-millisecond audio segment beginning 10 milliseconds before each detected impact will be extracted from the microphone with the highest signal-to-noise ratio. The following features will be calculated:

- peak amplitude;
- attack duration;
- spectral centroid;
- spectral roll-off at 85% of energy;
- high-to-low frequency energy ratio;
- harmonic concentration;
- zero-crossing rate;
- decay slope; and
- agreement in arrival time across microphones.

Features will be normalized relative to the median of their match so that venue temperature, audience size, and microphone gain do not dominate the measure. Principal component analysis will reduce the features to three components. An elastic-net regression will then predict a shuttle’s normalized position in its use cycle, defined as impact number divided by the total number of impacts before replacement. The predicted value, scaled from zero to one, will be SAAS.

For example, an impact with SAAS of 0.80 will be interpreted as acoustically similar to a shuttle that is four-fifths of the way through its usable life. A threshold of 0.65 will represent meaningful wear in the policy analysis. If a shuttle’s score falls temporarily, the rolling median of the last three contacts will be used, because physical aging should not reverse during a use cycle.

The first 48 matches will form the development sample and the final 24 the test sample. Predictive performance will be summarized with mean absolute error, correlation between SAAS and normalized use position, and accuracy in distinguishing the first and final thirds of a cycle. The primary tactical models will use scores generated for all impacts after the acoustic model has been selected, because using the full set will provide more stable values.

A supplementary calibration session will be conducted before the competition. Six participants will each play 100 machine-fed overhead strokes using new shuttles. Every shuttle will receive 25 strokes unless it visibly breaks. These data will verify that spectral features generally move in the same direction under repeated impacts, although the competition recordings will remain the basis of the final score.

## 5. Outcomes

The primary tactical outcome will be an attacking-shot indicator. Full smashes, half-smashes, and fast drives will be coded as attacking; all other strokes will be coded as non-attacking. The primary performance outcome will be whether the striker ultimately wins the rally. Secondary outcomes will include exit speed, landing depth, rally duration, immediate winner or forced error, and the probability of a replacement request within the next two rallies.

An **Attacking Efficiency Index** will also be calculated for each five-impact window:

`AEI = attacking-shot proportion × mean exit speed × rally-win proportion`

Each component will be converted to a value between zero and one before multiplication. This index is intended to identify periods in which a player attacks frequently, strikes quickly, and converts those attacks into points. Five-impact windows that cross a shuttle replacement will be discarded.

For H4, the main request-advantage outcome will be the proportion of the three points immediately after the first request in a cycle that are won by the requesting player. Both accepted and rejected first requests will be included. If a game ends before three further points, the available points will be used.

## 6. Statistical analysis

### 6.1 Sample size

Pilot scoring suggests an average of 55 rallies per match and approximately six recorded contacts per rally. Seventy-two matches should therefore provide about 23,760 impacts. Allowing for 10% unusable audio leaves roughly 21,000 observations. Assuming a clustering design effect of 1.6, the effective sample will be about 13,000 impacts. This is expected to provide 80% power to detect an odds ratio of 1.08 for the association between SAAS and attacking-shot choice at a two-sided 5% significance level.

No separate power calculation will be conducted for replacement requests because their number depends on player behavior. If fewer than 60 requests occur, accepted and rejected requests will be combined.

### 6.2 Acoustic and flight models

H1 will be evaluated by plotting SAAS against impact number and testing the slope in a mixed linear model. Shuttle identity and player will receive random intercepts. A change-point model will test whether the slope becomes steeper near impact 18. Evidence for acoustic aging will consist of a positive slope and test-sample correlation above 0.60.

For H2, shuttle exit speed will be regressed on SAAS, racket swing speed, stroke type, player, and game number. The principal coefficient will be interpreted as the speed lost through wear. Contacts for which camera tracking fails will be retained by substituting the mean exit speed for the relevant stroke type, and an indicator for imputation will be included.

### 6.3 Tactical model

H3 will use a mixed-effects logistic regression predicting whether each stroke is attacking. Fixed effects will include SAAS, score difference, rally contact number, whether the player is serving, game number, and the previous stroke category. Random intercepts will be added for player and match. A SAAS-by-player interaction will identify players whose tactics are especially sensitive to worn shuttles.

The progression of wear is treated as a natural within-match exposure. Because every shuttle starts near SAAS zero and tends to rise, comparison within a match should reduce bias from general player ability. Score difference is included to account for the possibility that trailing players attack more. A secondary model will replace continuous SAAS with early, middle, and late thirds of a use cycle.

Rally success will be modeled at the stroke level by assigning every stroke the final win or loss of its rally. A logistic model will test whether the SAAS value at each stroke predicts whether its striker wins the rally. Marginal predicted probabilities will be reported for SAAS values of 0.10, 0.50, and 0.90. Strokes in the same rally will be handled through match-level random effects.

The AEI analysis will compare five-impact windows above and below the 0.65 wear threshold using paired tests within players. If the index falls by at least 10%, the deterioration will be considered tactically meaningful.

### 6.4 Replacement requests and momentum

For H4, points following a first replacement request will be compared with the three points preceding it. A difference-in-differences calculation will contrast the requesting player’s before-to-after change against the opponent’s change. Separate estimates will be produced for accepted and rejected requests and for requests above and below SAAS 0.65.

A positive effect after both accepted and rejected requests will be interpreted as evidence that initiating the process creates a psychological or momentum advantage. An effect only after accepted requests will indicate that a fresher shuttle benefits the player who noticed wear first. Models will adjust for score margin and which player serves the next point.

### 6.5 Replacement policy simulation

The observed sequence of every match will be replayed under four policies:

1. current player-and-umpire judgment;
2. automatic replacement every 20 impacts;
3. automatic replacement when rolling SAAS exceeds 0.65; and
4. automatic replacement when predicted AEI loss exceeds 10%.

For each policy, the simulator will estimate shuttles consumed, number of impacts played above the wear threshold, and expected points shifted by deterioration. Expected point shifts will be calculated from the fitted rally-success model by replacing each observed worn-shuttle probability with its predicted probability at SAAS 0.10. A policy score will be computed as:

`Policy score = avoided shifted points − 0.04 × additional shuttles used`

The weight of 0.04 expresses the assumption that preventing one wear-shifted point is worth up to 25 extra shuttles across the tournament. The policy with the highest score will be recommended, with alternative weights of 0.02 and 0.08 shown as sensitivity checks.

False alarms will be defined as replacements triggered below impact 10 when no visible feather damage is recorded. Misses will be cycles in which SAAS remains below 0.65 despite reaching at least 25 impacts. This will allow organizers to understand both competitive and material costs.

## 7. Data quality and reproducibility

Before the series, microphones will be checked using the same recorded impulse at four court positions. Sensor clocks will be resynchronized before each game. Analysts coding video will not see SAAS values, replacement-request notes, or the eventual winner of the match. Inter-coder agreement below 0.75 for any major stroke category will trigger joint review and recoding of that category.

Hypotheses, exclusions, features, and primary models will be registered before the first competition match. Analysis scripts and a de-identified stroke-level table will be released after the project. Raw video will not be released because players may be recognizable. Short audio segments will be converted to feature values before sharing, reducing both storage requirements and the possibility of capturing intelligible conversation.

## 8. Ethics and participant burden

Participants will provide written consent for recording and sensor use. They may request deletion of close-up video captured between rallies, but deletion of in-play performance data after the analysis begins will not be possible because it would disrupt shuttle cycles. Players will receive a fixed appearance payment rather than payment based on wins.

The racket sensor adds less than six grams and will be fitted during a familiarization session. Participants who believe it changes racket balance may withdraw from sensor recording while remaining in the competition; their audio and video data can still be included. The acoustic system will not be used to overrule players or umpires during the study.

## 9. Schedule and resources

Months 1 and 2 will cover equipment construction, software testing, recruitment, and the machine-fed calibration session. Months 3 and 4 will contain the six competition weekends and initial quality checks. Months 5 and 6 will cover video coding and construction of SAAS. Statistical modeling and simulation will take place in Months 7 and 8, followed by reporting in Month 9.

The requested budget is 34,600 Northbridge credits: 9,000 for hall hire, 7,200 for participant payments, 5,800 for cameras and storage, 4,400 for microphones and synchronization equipment, 3,600 for shuttles, and 4,600 for research-assistant coding time. Existing racket sensors and analysis computers will be supplied by the Northbridge Shuttle Lab.

## 10. Expected contribution

The project will introduce a continuous equipment-condition variable into badminton analytics. Rather than describing a shuttle only as present or replaced, SAAS will locate every stroke on an estimated wear trajectory. This may improve models of shot selection and explain tactical changes that conventional score-based analyses leave unaccounted for.

For tournament organizers, the project will provide a direct comparison of judgment-led and automatic replacement systems. A microphone-based system would not require players to stop for physical inspection and might reduce disputes over replacement. Coaches could also use acoustic trajectories to examine whether particular players recognize deterioration early or adapt their shot selection effectively.

The synchronized dataset will support further work on impact detection, racket acoustics, and rally segmentation. Although the immediate study concerns one shuttle model and one venue, the same feature-extraction procedure could later be applied to doubles, junior competition, or synthetic shuttles.

## 11. Limitations

Contact sound is influenced by shot type, racket strings, impact position, microphone angle, and hall noise as well as shuttle condition. Match-level normalization and adjustment for coded stroke type should reduce these influences, while use of the strongest microphone should maintain signal quality. The study does not physically test drag or feather stiffness after every rally because such tests would interrupt play.

Replacement is also chosen by players and umpires rather than assigned randomly. The analysis addresses this through within-match comparison, score adjustment, and separate treatment of accepted and rejected requests. Findings will apply most directly to advanced club singles played with the Aerius F12. Replication would be needed before selecting one acoustic threshold for all standards of badminton.
